overview: This bill expands federal whistleblower protections for people who work on government contracts and grants. Under current law, employees of federal contractors and grantees cannot be fired, demoted, or otherwise punished for reporting fraud, waste, abuse, or legal violations involving federal money; this bill extends that protection to the contractors and grantees themselves, to former employees, to people working under personal services contracts, and to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments and intelligence agencies that receive federal contracts or grants. It also protects people who refuse an order that would require them to break a contract-related law or rule. It says federal officials have no authority to ask a contractor to retaliate against a whistleblower, allows the agency head to propose discipline for an official who does, and bars these rights from being waived, including through arbitration agreements signed in advance. It covers the Defense Department and NASA as well as other federal agencies. As of May 21, 2026, the Senate had passed it and it was awaiting action in the House.
for: Supporters say the bill closes gaps that let whistleblowers be punished indirectly, for example when a government official pressures a contractor to retaliate, and helps uncover waste and fraud in federal spending.
against: Critics say widening who is covered and barring arbitration agreements could expose contractors and grantees to more complaints and legal disputes, adding costs to federal contracting.
